I'd say the latter is clearer to me (function section), while the former relies on currying. The latter is (in this case) shorter as well.

I see a few occurrences of Prod.mk x around the code base. (A guess is because function section comes later, but I haven't checked this.)

Thought about changing it to the other form? (if not, there are a few occurrences of Prod.mk x y which is even clearer to change to (x, y))

I agree that (x, ·) and (x, y) look cleaner. Generally, the anonymous function syntax with (·) isn't that old so some of this might have historical reasons for inconsistency.

But then again, this is a formatting-question, and anything about (auto-) formatting is currently on hold waiting for the FRO-autoformatter in order to see what it is able to do and then build on top of it. So it's probably not recommended to make large-scale style refactors like this until it can be implemented in a fully-automated way which is compatible with the FRO-autoformatter...
Yeah I don't think this will be resolved by the formatter
Agreed. But it's not hard to write a syntax canonicalizer on top of it (and this is something Marc Huisinga , the formatter's author, also mentioned himself): so this could be in its extended scope.
Note that ⟨x, y⟩ is also possible. Given how many uses round parentheses have and given that angle brackets are used for tuples and nothing else, I vote for ⟨x, y⟩ being the canonical form.
Huh, angle brackets are for constructing any structure, not just tuple, no?
All structures are tuples in a sense, aren't they? I don' think that the fact that Prod isn't dependent makes it too different.

Martin Dvořák said:

Note that ⟨x, y⟩ is also possible. Given how many uses round parentheses have and given that angle brackets are used for tuples and nothing else, I vote for ⟨x, y⟩ being the canonical form.

But what about fun y => Prod.mk x y? How would you write this function?
You can (⟨x, ·⟩) I guess, but doesn't look very elegant.

Martin Dvořák said:

given that angle brackets are used for tuples and nothing else ... all structures are tuples in a sense, aren't they?

You think of docs#Filter as a tuple in your normal mathematical practice? I would argue that you shouldn't.
Although isn't it great that the third coordinate of the rational number 1 / 2 is a bijection
I don't think of filters in my normal mathematical practice at all. In Lean, I definitely think of docs#Filter as a tuple. Any inductive type with a single constructor is a tuple for me.

Aaron Liu said:

But what about fun y => Prod.mk x y? How would you write this function?

Good point. I'd probably write Prod.mk x rather than notation.

I agree that (⟨x, ·⟩) look bad and that (x, ·) looks a lot cleaner (tho it creeps me out because my brain immediately parses those parentheses as a function notation (because of the dot) and fails to see that the parentheses denote a Prod at the same time).

Martin Dvořák said:

Any inductive type with a single constructor is a tuple for me.

The reason this is so strange is that you are conflating the type itself with its implementation. For example, Filter could just as well have been implemented as a quotient type, and then not only wouldn't it have a single constructor, it wouldn't be an inductive type at all! Nevertheless, it would still be capable of serving the same purpose in the library.

To take an example with which you are certainly familiar: docs#Int is implemented as an inductive type, but it just as well could have been implemented as a quotient of Nat × Nat (which is how I generally present the construction to my students), disregarding the fact that there are good computational reasons to prefer the inductive approach.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Martin Dvořák said:

Any inductive type with a single constructor is a tuple for me.

The reason this is so strange is that you are conflating the type itself with its implementation.

For me, a mathematical object is what its formal definition says. The other things you talk about are ways of thinking about the object in my mind.

Sorry for the tangent... I have a feeling that there are generally two schools of MathematiCS:
(a) There is one definition. It may have many equivalent characterizations.
(b) There is one concept. The concept may have many equivalent definitions.
